sections.heading: Key points
sections.content:
*   Two million-person studies found shared addiction risk and personality–substance links.
*   There is no single addictive personality. Multiple traits create multiple pathways to addiction.
*   Some people seek stimulation. Others seek relief. Repeated exposure can overwhelm either pathway.
*   Risk is not destiny. Treat the person and the pathway—not a supposedly defective personality.

Two enormous genetic studies have reopened one of [addiction](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/addiction "Psychology Today looks at addiction") psychiatry’s oldest debates: Is the "addictive [personality](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/personality "Psychology Today looks at personality")" a valid concept?

In September 2026, Ted Schwaba and colleagues analyzed the [genetics](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/genetics "Psychology Today looks at genetics") of the [Big Five](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/big-5-personality-traits "Psychology Today looks at Big Five") personality traits in 1.14 million people. They identified 1,260 associated genetic variants, including 824 that had not been reported before. Some genetic signals overlapped with substance use. Genetic liability to [conscientiousness](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/conscientiousness "Psychology Today looks at conscientiousness") was correlated with less substance use across substances. Higher [neuroticism](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/neuroticism "Psychology Today looks at neuroticism") was linked with several substance outcomes, especially alcohol dependence. Higher [agreeableness](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/agreeableness "Psychology Today looks at agreeableness") was generally protective against addiction.

Three years earlier, Alexander Hatoum and more than 150 colleagues analyzed data from over 1.1 million people. They found a general addiction risk factor spanning problematic alcohol and tobacco use, cannabis use disorder, and opioid use disorder. They also found substance-specific risks. Shared vulnerability, _yes_. One addiction gene, _no_.

Put the studies together, and the answer seems new, exciting, and strangely familiar: Personality matters. So do genes. But neither study gives us a test capable of identifying those who will become addicted.

Genome-wide association studies detect patterns across populations. They don’t read any single individual's mind. A polygenic score is not a diagnosis and it certainly is no crystal ball. It is also not equally accurate across ancestries.

sections.heading: Three Thousand Years of Addiction Explanations
sections.content:
For three millennia, people have tried to explain why some lose control while others do not. The data was dwarfed by the ever-changing explanations.

Ancient Western traditions emphasized excess, [wisdom](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/wisdom "Psychology Today looks at wisdom"), character, reason, or self-command. Early Buddhist thought emphasized something different: craving and [attachment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attachment "Psychology Today looks at attachment") as universal human processes—not evidence of a defective class of people. Aristotle called acting against one’s better judgment _akrasia_. Benjamin Rush later moved habitual drunkenness away from simple sin and toward disease and loss of control

![Image 15: History of Addictive Personality](https://cdn2.psychologytoday.com/assets/styles/article_inline_full_caption/public/field_blog_entry_images/2026-09/history_of_addictive_personality_0.png.jpg?itok=DvmHsmsu)

History of Addictive Personality

Source: Mark Gold, MD

In an 1897 letter to Wilhelm Fliess, [Freud](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/freudian-psychology "Psychology Today looks at Freud") called [masturbation](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/masturbation "Psychology Today looks at masturbation") the “primal addiction” and viewed alcohol, morphine, and tobacco as substitutes. In that same letter, however, he wondered whether addiction was curable—or whether “analysis and [therapy](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/therapy "Psychology Today looks at therapy") must come to a halt.”

In 1933, [psychoanalyst](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychoanalysis "Psychology Today looks at psychoanalyst") Sándor Radó published his famous paper calling addiction “pharmacothymia,” or a chemical shortcut for changing a painful mood. The word has disappeared, but the observation has not. People do not always take drugs to feel good. Often, they take them to stop feeling bad.

sections.heading: The Alcoholic Personality Problem
sections.content:
Then emerged the search for the alcoholic personality. Some patients were said to be primarily impulsive, [sensation-seeking](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/sensation-seeking "Psychology Today looks at sensation-seeking"), and antisocial. Others were anxious, inhibited, depressed, or compulsive. Some appeared quite ordinary until alcohol reorganized their lives. Yet all supposedly shared one personality. This was convenient. Also, circular: People drank because they had an alcoholic personality. How did we know? They drank.

Jellinek’s disease model recognized that different people travel different roads to the same disorder. For [alcoholism](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/alcohol "Psychology Today looks at alcoholism"), Cloninger later proposed an earlier-onset, more heritable and externalizing pathway and a later-onset, anxious and harm-avoidant pathway.

In this tradition, Harvard’s Edward Khantzian made the relief pathway clinically useful. His self-[medication](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychopharmacology "Psychology Today looks at medication") hypothesis asked a better question: Why does this drug fit this person? Opioids may quiet [rage](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anger "Psychology Today looks at rage") or dysphoria. Stimulants may temporarily provide energy, [confidence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/confidence "Psychology Today looks at confidence"), or focus. Alcohol and benzodiazepines may reduce worrying or hyperarousal. The drug then becomes a crude prescription—fast, effective, and eventually destructive. The attempted solution becomes the disease. Ken Blum’s reward deficiency syndrome asked why ordinary rewards may not be rewarding enough.

sections.heading: What the Genetics Changes
sections.content:
Epidemiological studies tell us that about half the risk for addiction is genetic; vulnerability seems to be roughly the same for all drugs. A 50 percent genetic risk is higher than for type II diabetes or hypertension, which we often think of as genetic diseases.

Sensation seeking or reward deficiency may open the door. [Anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at Anxiety"), [anhedonia](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anhedonia "Psychology Today looks at anhedonia"), [ADHD](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/adhd "Psychology Today looks at ADHD"), [trauma](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/trauma "Psychology Today looks at trauma"), or [insomnia](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/insomnia "Psychology Today looks at insomnia") may influence the drug of choice. Then repeated use, potency, and brain adaptation may overwhelm the original vulnerabilities. Genes may influence vulnerability, but exposure remains required: No first use or exposure, no addiction.

article continues after advertisement

The new genetics replaces a pejorative label with multiple pathways to risk.

Who experiments? Who finds a particular drug unusually useful? Who, after repeated exposure, cannot stop? No single trait answers all three questions.

Old AA wisdom said alcoholism “skipped a generation.” Genes do not skip generations, but the child of an alcoholic may have seen way too much, and so avoided alcohol entirely. The vulnerability may have remained, but without use, alcohol was never a problem. A grandchild who drank could make the family history appear to skip a generation: Genes were transmitted, but exposure was not.

Higher neuroticism may increase interest in drugs promising relief. Lower conscientiousness may make planning, delaying gratification, and resisting immediate reward harder. Higher conscientiousness and agreeableness may offer some protection. _May_, not _must_.

Personality can influence experimentation, drug choice, and stopping. But personality before addiction should not be confused with behavior during intoxication, withdrawal, craving, or desperation. Someone [lying](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/deception "Psychology Today looks at lying") to obtain heroin is not necessarily a dishonest person. Heroin dependence can make honesty extraordinarily expensive.

The drug matters too. Fentanyl can addict anyone, even a careful anesthesiologist. Alcohol can trap a conscientious physician. Cocaine can overwhelm a successful, motivated person. Potency, availability, age at first exposure, trauma, [psychiatric](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychiatry "Psychology Today looks at psychiatric") illness, peers, and brain adaptation all matter.

Personality is part of the story. It is not the whole story.

sections.heading: Why This Matters Today
sections.content:
The addictive personality label survives because it is simple. It turns risk into [identity](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/identity "Psychology Today looks at identity"). It also suggests that people with addiction are defective—and safely different from the rest of us.

The genetics tells a less comfortable—and more democratic—story. Risk is spread across the population, shared partly across drugs, and changed by development and exposure.

Risk is not destiny, and behavior in the middle of addiction should not become a lifetime description of a person.

This changes treatment: Do not treat a mythical addictive personality. Treat the pathway to addiction and treat the individual.

A sensation-seeking adolescent may need structure, alternative rewards, and reduced drug access. A traumatized patient using opioids for emotional anesthesia needs evidence-based addiction treatment and trauma-informed care. ADHD, [depression](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/depression "Psychology Today looks at depression"), anxiety, and insomnia need treatment—not dismissal as excuses. Patients whose lives have narrowed to drug reward need medication, recovery support, and help rebuilding ordinary rewards.

article continues after advertisement

Prevention should follow the same logic. Delay first exposure to substances. Reduce access to potent drugs. Treat psychiatric illness early. Strengthen families and schools. Genetics may eventually sharpen prevention. Today, it already teaches humility.

So, is there one addictive personality? No. There is no single defective personality shared by everyone with addiction. Instead, multiple partly heritable traits alter risk through different pathways—and then there is the drug, the dose, [the environment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/environment "Psychology Today looks at the environment"), and time.

That answer is less catchy than “the addictive personality.” It is also more accurate, less stigmatizing, and far more useful.

# Is the "Addictive Personality" Real?

## Can you have an "addictive personality"? Yes and no. Here are the facts.

### Key points

*   Two million-person studies found shared addiction risk and personality–substance links.
*   There is no single addictive personality. Multiple traits create multiple pathways to addiction.
*   Some people seek stimulation. Others seek relief. Repeated exposure can overwhelm either pathway.
*   Risk is not destiny. Treat the person and the pathway—not a supposedly defective personality.

Two enormous genetic studies have reopened one of [addiction](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/addiction "Psychology Today looks at addiction") psychiatry’s oldest debates: Is the "addictive [personality](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/personality "Psychology Today looks at personality")" a valid concept?

In September 2026, Ted Schwaba and colleagues analyzed the [genetics](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/genetics "Psychology Today looks at genetics") of the [Big Five](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/big-5-personality-traits "Psychology Today looks at Big Five") personality traits in 1.14 million people. They identified 1,260 associated genetic variants, including 824 that had not been reported before. Some genetic signals overlapped with substance use. Genetic liability to [conscientiousness](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/conscientiousness "Psychology Today looks at conscientiousness") was correlated with less substance use across substances. Higher [neuroticism](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/neuroticism "Psychology Today looks at neuroticism") was linked with several substance outcomes, especially alcohol dependence. Higher [agreeableness](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/agreeableness "Psychology Today looks at agreeableness") was generally protective against addiction.

Three years earlier, Alexander Hatoum and more than 150 colleagues analyzed data from over 1.1 million people. They found a general addiction risk factor spanning problematic alcohol and tobacco use, cannabis use disorder, and opioid use disorder. They also found substance-specific risks. Shared vulnerability, _yes_. One addiction gene, _no_.

Put the studies together, and the answer seems new, exciting, and strangely familiar: Personality matters. So do genes. But neither study gives us a test capable of identifying those who will become addicted.

Genome-wide association studies detect patterns across populations. They don’t read any single individual's mind. A polygenic score is not a diagnosis and it certainly is no crystal ball. It is also not equally accurate across ancestries.

## Three Thousand Years of Addiction Explanations

For three millennia, people have tried to explain why some lose control while others do not. The data was dwarfed by the ever-changing explanations.

Ancient Western traditions emphasized excess, [wisdom](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/wisdom "Psychology Today looks at wisdom"), character, reason, or self-command. Early Buddhist thought emphasized something different: craving and [attachment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/attachment "Psychology Today looks at attachment") as universal human processes—not evidence of a defective class of people. Aristotle called acting against one’s better judgment _akrasia_. Benjamin Rush later moved habitual drunkenness away from simple sin and toward disease and loss of control

In an 1897 letter to Wilhelm Fliess, [Freud](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/freudian-psychology "Psychology Today looks at Freud") called [masturbation](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/masturbation "Psychology Today looks at masturbation") the “primal addiction” and viewed alcohol, morphine, and tobacco as substitutes. In that same letter, however, he wondered whether addiction was curable—or whether “analysis and [therapy](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/therapy "Psychology Today looks at therapy") must come to a halt.”

In 1933, [psychoanalyst](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychoanalysis "Psychology Today looks at psychoanalyst") Sándor Radó published his famous paper calling addiction “pharmacothymia,” or a chemical shortcut for changing a painful mood. The word has disappeared, but the observation has not. People do not always take drugs to feel good. Often, they take them to stop feeling bad.

## The Alcoholic Personality Problem

Then emerged the search for the alcoholic personality. Some patients were said to be primarily impulsive, [sensation-seeking](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/sensation-seeking "Psychology Today looks at sensation-seeking"), and antisocial. Others were anxious, inhibited, depressed, or compulsive. Some appeared quite ordinary until alcohol reorganized their lives. Yet all supposedly shared one personality. This was convenient. Also, circular: People drank because they had an alcoholic personality. How did we know? They drank.

Jellinek’s disease model recognized that different people travel different roads to the same disorder. For [alcoholism](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/alcohol "Psychology Today looks at alcoholism"), Cloninger later proposed an earlier-onset, more heritable and externalizing pathway and a later-onset, anxious and harm-avoidant pathway.

In this tradition, Harvard’s Edward Khantzian made the relief pathway clinically useful. His self-[medication](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychopharmacology "Psychology Today looks at medication") hypothesis asked a better question: Why does this drug fit this person? Opioids may quiet [rage](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anger "Psychology Today looks at rage") or dysphoria. Stimulants may temporarily provide energy, [confidence](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/confidence "Psychology Today looks at confidence"), or focus. Alcohol and benzodiazepines may reduce worrying or hyperarousal. The drug then becomes a crude prescription—fast, effective, and eventually destructive. The attempted solution becomes the disease. Ken Blum’s reward deficiency syndrome asked why ordinary rewards may not be rewarding enough.

## What the Genetics Changes

Epidemiological studies tell us that about half the risk for addiction is genetic; vulnerability seems to be roughly the same for all drugs. A 50 percent genetic risk is higher than for type II diabetes or hypertension, which we often think of as genetic diseases.

Sensation seeking or reward deficiency may open the door. [Anxiety](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anxiety "Psychology Today looks at Anxiety"), [anhedonia](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/anhedonia "Psychology Today looks at anhedonia"), [ADHD](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/adhd "Psychology Today looks at ADHD"), [trauma](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/trauma "Psychology Today looks at trauma"), or [insomnia](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/insomnia "Psychology Today looks at insomnia") may influence the drug of choice. Then repeated use, potency, and brain adaptation may overwhelm the original vulnerabilities. Genes may influence vulnerability, but exposure remains required: No first use or exposure, no addiction.

The new genetics replaces a pejorative label with multiple pathways to risk.

Who experiments? Who finds a particular drug unusually useful? Who, after repeated exposure, cannot stop? No single trait answers all three questions.

Old AA wisdom said alcoholism “skipped a generation.” Genes do not skip generations, but the child of an alcoholic may have seen way too much, and so avoided alcohol entirely. The vulnerability may have remained, but without use, alcohol was never a problem. A grandchild who drank could make the family history appear to skip a generation: Genes were transmitted, but exposure was not.

Higher neuroticism may increase interest in drugs promising relief. Lower conscientiousness may make planning, delaying gratification, and resisting immediate reward harder. Higher conscientiousness and agreeableness may offer some protection. _May_, not _must_.

Personality can influence experimentation, drug choice, and stopping. But personality before addiction should not be confused with behavior during intoxication, withdrawal, craving, or desperation. Someone [lying](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/deception "Psychology Today looks at lying") to obtain heroin is not necessarily a dishonest person. Heroin dependence can make honesty extraordinarily expensive.

The drug matters too. Fentanyl can addict anyone, even a careful anesthesiologist. Alcohol can trap a conscientious physician. Cocaine can overwhelm a successful, motivated person. Potency, availability, age at first exposure, trauma, [psychiatric](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/psychiatry "Psychology Today looks at psychiatric") illness, peers, and brain adaptation all matter.

Personality is part of the story. It is not the whole story.

## Why This Matters Today

The addictive personality label survives because it is simple. It turns risk into [identity](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/identity "Psychology Today looks at identity"). It also suggests that people with addiction are defective—and safely different from the rest of us.

The genetics tells a less comfortable—and more democratic—story. Risk is spread across the population, shared partly across drugs, and changed by development and exposure.

Risk is not destiny, and behavior in the middle of addiction should not become a lifetime description of a person.

This changes treatment: Do not treat a mythical addictive personality. Treat the pathway to addiction and treat the individual.

A sensation-seeking adolescent may need structure, alternative rewards, and reduced drug access. A traumatized patient using opioids for emotional anesthesia needs evidence-based addiction treatment and trauma-informed care. ADHD, [depression](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/depression "Psychology Today looks at depression"), anxiety, and insomnia need treatment—not dismissal as excuses. Patients whose lives have narrowed to drug reward need medication, recovery support, and help rebuilding ordinary rewards.

Prevention should follow the same logic. Delay first exposure to substances. Reduce access to potent drugs. Treat psychiatric illness early. Strengthen families and schools. Genetics may eventually sharpen prevention. Today, it already teaches humility.

So, is there one addictive personality? No. There is no single defective personality shared by everyone with addiction. Instead, multiple partly heritable traits alter risk through different pathways—and then there is the drug, the dose, [the environment](https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/basics/environment "Psychology Today looks at the environment"), and time.

That answer is less catchy than “the addictive personality.” It is also more accurate, less stigmatizing, and far more useful.
